subject: Speed up ddply but keep the elegance?

messages.author: 3a775dfa0a96bf95
messages.subject: Speed up ddply but keep the elegance?
parts:
I was trying to use ddply/subset/order to find the max element of each small group in a 300,000-row dataset, and found that it was slow.  See below for specifics.

There is a much faster way (x100) to do things using sorting (see below), but it is nowhere near as elegant as the ddply method.

Is there some way to combine the speed of the fast technique with the elegance of the ddply approach?

            -s

----------------------------------

testdff <- function (n) { s <- sample(n); data.frame(a=floor(s/5),b=s) }

testn.ddply.order <-  function (n) {
  dff <- testdff(n)
  system.time(ddply(dff,.(a),function(d) d[order(d$b)==1,]))
}

testn.ddply.subset.order <-  function (n) {
  dff <- testdff(n)
  system.time(ddply(dff,.(a),subset,order(b)==1))
}

breaks <- function(s) if(length(s)==0) logical(0) else c(TRUE,s[-1] != s[-length(s)])

groupmax <- function (dff,groupcol,maxcol) {
  xx <- dff[order(dff[,groupcol],desc(dff[,maxcol])),]
  xx[breaks(xx[,groupcol]),] }

testn.order <- function (n) {
  dff <- testdff(n)
  system.time(groupmax(dff,"a","b"))
}

> testn.ddply.order(10000)
   user  system elapsed 
   0.92    0.00    0.92 
> testn.ddply.subset.order(10000)
   user  system elapsed 
   1.09    0.00    1.12     --- relatively small overhead for using subset
> testn.order(10000)
   user  system elapsed 
      0       0       0           -- but using order/breaks is much faster
> testn.order(1000000)
   user  system elapsed 
   1.34    0.00    1.35     -- almost 100x
